summary: Kerberos 5 can use DES encryption, which NIST withdrew in 2005 and which is weak enough to break with modest hardware. This best current practice deprecates DES, RC4-HMAC-EXP and other weak algorithms in Kerberos.

plainLanguage.summary: An old lock that burglars can pick with cheap tools should be thrown away. This tells Kerberos to stop using its weak locks.

subtitle: Retire weak encryption in Kerberos before it becomes a liability.

tldr.problem: The Kerberos 5 protocol originally supported only DES encryption, a 56-bit cipher that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) officially withdrew in 2005. By 2008, hardware costing less than USD 15,000 could break DES keys in less than a day. Kerberos also supports other weak algorithms like RC4-HMAC-EXP (56-bit export strength) and unencrypted checksums.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6649 updates the Kerberos specifications and GSS-API mechanisms to deprecate DES, RC4-HMAC-EXP, and other weak cryptographic algorithms. It recommends reclassification of the original RFC 1510 (which only supports DES) as Historic, and updates RFC 1964, RFC 4120, RFC 4121, and RFC 4757 to discourage use of weak algorithms.
tldr.outcome: Deployments are encouraged to remove support for weak encryption types, ensuring Kerberos uses only modern, secure algorithms. The document acknowledges a transition period for legacy Microsoft Windows systems but makes clear that DES is no longer appropriate for any use.

today: RFC 6649 is a Best Current Practice document that updates RFC 1964, RFC 4120, RFC 4121, and RFC 4757 to deprecate weak cryptographic algorithms in Kerberos. It has not been obsoleted. Modern Kerberos deployments should no longer use DES or RC4-HMAC-EXP; RFC 1510 is now classified as Historic.

sections.title: Why DES Is No Longer Safe
sections.content:
The original Kerberos 5 specification (RFC 1510) supported only the Data Encryption Standard (DES), a 56-bit cipher published in 1977. Even then, cryptographers questioned whether 56 bits was too small. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) formally withdrew DES in 2005, acknowledging decades of consensus that it was no longer secure.

By 2006, researchers had demonstrated breaking DES in less than 9 days with hardware costing under EUR 10,000. By 2008, companies offered hardware for less than USD 15,000 that could crack a DES key in less than a day on average. DES brute-force attacks only get faster and cheaper as hardware improves.

This document recommends treating RFC 1510 as Historic and updates four Kerberos-related specifications to deprecate DES and other weak cryptographic algorithms, including RC4-HMAC-EXP (another export-strength, 56-bit cipher) and various unencrypted or weak checksums.
sections.plainLanguage: DES is an old encryption method with a tiny key. Researchers have shown how to break it with ordinary hardware in less than a day. It is time to stop using it.

sections.title: Which Kerberos Specifications Are Affected
sections.content:
RFC 1510 (September 1993) specified Kerberos 5 with DES as the only encryption algorithm. RFC 4120 (2005) obsoleted RFC 1510 and added modern encryption types to Kerberos but still permitted DES. RFC 3961 describes the Kerberos cryptographic framework and includes DES support but does not specify requirement levels for any algorithm.

RFC 1964 (1996) and RFC 4121 (2005) specify the Kerberos Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface (GSS-API) mechanism, which defines DES-based integrity and confidentiality mechanisms. Modern alternatives (RC4-HMAC, DES3, and others) exist, making DES-based GSS-API mechanisms unnecessary.

RFC 4757 (2006) describes Microsoft's RC4-HMAC encryption types and includes a 56-bit export-strength variant called RC4-HMAC-EXP.

This document updates RFC 1964, RFC 4120, RFC 4121, and RFC 4757 to clarify that weak algorithms SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Different versions of Kerberos used DES in different ways. This RFC tells all of them to stop using DES and other weak methods.

sections.title: Which Algorithms Are Deprecated
sections.content:
The document removes the RECOMMENDED status from DES-CBC-MD5 (encryption type 3) in RFC 4120. Kerberos implementations and deployments SHOULD NOT implement or deploy these single DES encryption types: DES-CBC-CRC (type 1), DES-CBC-MD4 (type 2), and DES-CBC-MD5 (type 3).

RC4-HMAC-EXP (encryption type 24), the export-strength 56-bit variant, is also deprecated. The document does not mandate RC4-HMAC (type 23), the 128-bit variant.

Several checksum types are deprecated: CRC32, RSA-MD4, RSA-MD4-DES, DES-MAC, DES-MAC-K, RSA-MD4-DES-K, and DES-MD5 (RSA-MD5-DES). These are unencrypted or tied to DES.

RSA-MD5 (type 7) is considered unsafe on its own but MAY be used inside an encrypted Authenticator for backward compatibility with legacy systems that do not support newer checksum types, particularly older Microsoft Windows systems that only support RC4-HMAC.

The GSS-API mechanisms deprecated include DES MAC MD5 (SGN ALG 0000), MD2.5 (0100), DES MAC (0200), and the DES SEAL ALG (0000) from RFC 1964.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the old locks to throw away: various ways to use DES in Kerberos, and a few other weak methods. There is one exception for old systems that need temporary help.

sections.title: Security Improvements
sections.content:
Removing single DES encryption directly improves security because DES is cryptographically broken. RC4-HMAC-EXP, with its 56-bit effective key size, has the same inadequate security profile and its removal is equally important.

Kerberos defines some encryption types that are either poorly specified or exist only by name without a published specification. Implementations should ensure they only use secure, well-specified encryption types.

RC4-HMAC (the 128-bit variant) is retained despite known weaknesses in RC4 and MD4 for one reason: it is the only encryption type that maintains interoperability with older Microsoft Windows releases once DES and RC4-HMAC-EXP are removed. These older Windows versions were expected to remain in use at least until 2015. The document does not change the Informational status of RFC 4757 for now.
sections.plainLanguage: Removing these weak locks makes Kerberos much safer. One exception is kept temporarily to work with old Windows computers that cannot use anything better.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Path
sections.content:
The recommendations use the RFC 2119 keywords SHOULD NOT and MAY, not MUST, to allow for a transition period. Implementations are encouraged (not mandated) to drop weak algorithms. Organizations with legacy systems still using DES or RC4-HMAC-EXP should plan their migration to modern algorithms.

The deprecation of RFC 1510 as Historic acknowledges that the original 1993 specification is obsolete and should not be referenced for new work. RFC 4120 supersedes it and is the authoritative specification, even though it still allows weak algorithms until they are fully removed from implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not say implementers MUST remove these locks immediately, but strongly encourages them to do so. Organizations need to plan how to move systems off the weak algorithms.
